slides: Let's continue with the number line, and see how operations move a number.

slides.say: How do multiplying and dividing move a positive number? Multiplying by a number bigger than one makes it grow. Nine times two is eighteen, and four times three is twelve.
Dividing by a number bigger than one makes it shrink. Ten divided by five is two, and twelve divided by four is three.
at: Ten divided by five is two

slides.say: Multiplying by a fraction between zero and one makes it shrink too, because we only take part of it. Ten times one fifth is two, and eight times one half is four.
at: Ten times one fifth is two

slides.say: Dividing by a fraction between zero and one is the opposite. Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by its reciprocal. So ten divided by one fifth is ten times five, which is fifty. And three divided by one half is three times two, which is six. The number grows.
at: So ten divided by one fifth
And three divided by one half

slides.say: So one is the dividing line. Times one or divided by one changes nothing. On the negative side, the same moves happen as a mirror image, away from zero or toward zero. Multiplying by a negative number is different, because it jumps to the other side of zero, and we'll see that in a later lesson.
at: So one is the dividing line

slides.say: Now the hierarchy. Take two positive numbers in different ranges, one above one and one between zero and one. A positive power or root keeps a positive number on its side of one. So the number above one stays bigger. For negative numbers, this works only with odd powers and odd roots. Here's an example. Which is bigger, the fifth root of eleven tenths, or the square root of seven ninths? Calculating these roots would be a nightmare, so we don't.
at: A positive power or root keeps

slides.say: Eleven tenths is bigger than one, because eleven is bigger than ten. A root of a number above one stays above one. Seven ninths is between zero and one, because seven is smaller than nine. Its root stays between zero and one too. So the fifth root of eleven tenths is bigger. We ignore the roots and look at the numbers themselves.
at: So the fifth root of eleven tenths is bigger

slides.say: Another one. Five quarters to the power of three, against the square root of three fifths. Five quarters is above one, so its cube is above one too. Three fifths is between zero and one, so its root is too. So five quarters to the power of three is bigger.
at: Five quarters to the power of three, against
So five quarters to the power of three is bigger

slides: Why only odd powers and roots for negative numbers? Because an even power makes a negative number positive. That's what we look at next.

slides.say: Some powers move a number into a different range. We call them exceptional powers, and we deal with them first. The first kind is a negative number to an even power. Negative five, squared, is twenty-five, and negative three, to the power of four, is eighty-one. Both jumped to the positive side.

Careful with the brackets. Negative five, in brackets, squared, is twenty-five. But without brackets, negative five squared means we square only the five, and then put the minus in front. That gives negative twenty-five.

The second kind is a negative exponent. We flip the base and drop the minus. Three eighths to the power of negative two is eight thirds, squared. The base was a fraction, and now it's above one. And five to the power of negative three is one fifth to the power of three. The base was above one, and now it's a fraction.
at: Three eighths to the power of negative
And five to the power of negative

slides.say: Here's how it helps. Which is bigger, the square root of four sevenths, or three fifths to the power of negative three? First handle the exceptional power: flip it, and it's five thirds to the power of three. Five thirds is above one, so its cube is above one. The square root of four sevenths is less than one. So three fifths to the power of negative three is bigger.
at: Which is bigger, the square root of four sevenths
So three fifths to the power of negative

slides: In the next lesson you'll meet the arrows, and with the arrows you may keep the minus in the exponent. Both ways give the same answer. [pause] I'll see you in the next part.
